intro.title: Stop chatting. Start delegating.
intro.lead: Thirteen ideas, one per screen. Each is a thing to point at while you explain. Cowork is Claude doing the work, in your files, your apps, your browser. Take the silences.
intro.teach:
Thirteen ideas, one screen each. The whole course turns on one move: you stop typing questions and start handing over work. Chat is where you think out loud.

Cowork is where you give Claude a job and it goes and does it, in your files, your apps, your browser. I'll show you, then I'll stop and ask where it fits your week.

close.title: Hand off the work. Teach it your way. Trust, but review.
close.lead: Cowork goes beyond chat to let you delegate real work. Make it yours with standing context, skills and plugins; run it across your browser and Office; then share what works and keep it safe.
close.teach:
If you keep one thing: hand off the work, don't just chat about it. Teach Cowork your way once, with global instructions, a project, a skill, and the next deliverable comes back better and faster. Trust it to do the doing, but review the result like a colleague's draft, because you own what goes out.

Everything we saw today, the browser, the Office apps, the marketplace, is a way to do that in more places.

steps.title: Chat thinks with you. Cowork does the work.
steps.cap: Chat is where you go to think out loud. Cowork is for the work you'd normally do yourself: describe an outcome and Claude plans, executes, and delivers the whole thing, context-gathering, analysis, file production, tool use.
steps.teach:
"Three versions of the same Claude. Chat is turn-by-turn, where you go to think out loud and draft. Cowork is different in kind, not degree: you describe a finished thing and Claude gathers the context, does the steps, uses your tools, and saves the deliverable back.

Code is for developers building software. The instinct from chatbots is one question, one answer, then you stitch the rest together yourself. Cowork takes the whole stitch off your plate." (The deck's caption: Chat is to think out loud, Cowork is for the work you'd normally do yourself.)

videos.label: Introducing Cowork: Claude Code for the rest of your work

checks.q: What actually changes when you move from Chat to Cowork?

options.t: It's the same conversation, given longer to run.
options.why: Time isn't the difference. Think about who does the steps in between the question and the deliverable.

options.t: It writes software rather than documents.
options.why: That's the third mode. Cowork isn't about what the output is made of.

options.t: You hand over an outcome, and it plans, runs the steps and delivers the whole thing.

checks.q: "Why not just use Claude in the browser?" What's the straight answer?

options.t: The browser forgets between sessions and struggles with a folder of files.
The browser sends your data somewhere the desktop doesn't.
options.why: Not the distinction here, and reaching for a safety answer to a convenience question tends to raise a fear rather than settle one.

options.t: The browser version is a smaller model.
options.why: Same intelligence on both. The difference is what it can hold on to and what it can reach.

steps.title: Point it at a folder. That folder is the boundary.
steps.cap: Install the desktop app, sign in, pick Cowork. The folder is the single most important choice, pick the smallest one that holds what the task needs. Cloud connectors are often read-only; your local folder is where Claude builds and iterates.
steps.teach:
"You install the desktop app, sign in, pick Cowork, then make one decision that matters more than any other: which folder. That folder is the boundary, the room Claude works in. Pick the smallest one that holds the task, not your whole Documents drive.

Connectors reach into your email, Drive and the rest, often read-only. And you choose how it asks: ask-before-acting is the default, and it always asks before deleting, no exceptions." (The deck's caption: cloud connectors are often read-only; your local folder is where Claude builds and iterates.)

checks.q: Three things get set up: the folder, the connectors, and how closely it asks before acting. Which one matters most?

options.t: The folder, because it's the boundary for everything it touches.
The connectors, because they decide what it can reach.
options.why: They widen the reach, and they don't bound it. Something else draws the line around everything it touches.

options.t: How closely it asks, because that's your control.
options.why: That's your comfort setting. It governs how often you're consulted, not what's within reach.

checks.q: A colleague asks what Cowork can see once it's running.

options.t: Only files you name in the prompt.
options.why: Too tight. It can work across the folder without you listing every file.

options.t: The folder you pointed it at, plus whatever your connectors reach and you can already see.
Anything on the machine, since it runs locally.
options.why: Running locally is not the same as being unbounded. One of the three setup choices exists precisely to stop that.

steps.title: Three kinds of work worth handing off
steps.cap: The through-line: work that used to mean juggling steps, files and tools in your head can now be handed off as a single task. Scheduled tasks and Dispatch only run when your computer is on and Claude is running.
steps.teach:
"How do you know a task is right for Cowork? Three patterns. It takes several steps, gather, compare, research, draft, format.

It lives in real files and ends in a real file. Or it spans the tools you already use. Hit one or more and it's a handoff.

And you don't have to be at your desk: you can schedule it to run weekly, or dispatch it from your phone, as long as your machine is on and Claude is running." (The deck's caption: the through-line is work you used to juggle in your head, handed off as a single task.)

videos.label: Scheduled Tasks in Cowork: Set it once, Claude handles the rest
Dispatch tasks to Claude Cowork from anywhere

checks.q: Which of these is the weakest candidate for handing to Cowork?

options.t: Pulling figures out of forty PDFs into one sheet.
options.why: File-based and repetitive, which is exactly the profile worth delegating.

options.t: Deciding which of two strategies the firm should back.
A weekly report that pulls from three different systems.
options.why: Multi-step and multi-tool. A strong candidate rather than a weak one.

checks.q: You schedule a task for 6am. Your laptop is shut. What happens?

options.t: It queues and runs the moment you open the lid.
options.why: Reasonable guess, and it promises a catch-up that isn't there.

options.t: It runs on Anthropic's servers and the result is waiting for you.
options.why: That's how a cloud service behaves. Cowork's scheduling has a condition attached that this misses.

options.t: Nothing. Scheduled tasks and Dispatch only run while your computer is on.

steps.eyebrow: Lesson 4, if you take one thing away
steps.title: Brief it like a smart colleague
steps.cap: More of the back-and-forth happens upfront, before Claude starts, instead of across five rounds of "actually, can you also…". The deliverable is the artifact, not the chat, check that it met the objective and that nothing's made up.
steps.teach:
Brief it the way you'd brief a capable colleague who's about to disappear into a task and come back with it done. Three things: name the deliverable, a one-page brief, a slide, a ranked list; name the inputs, which folder, which channel, which date range; and name the nuance only you would know.

It'll ask a question or two to close the gaps, then go. If it drifts, jump in, the cost of a redirect is low. Then you review the file, not the chat.

checks.q: A good Cowork brief names three things. Which is the one people leave out?

options.t: The nuance it could never guess.
The deliverable.
options.why: People are usually clear about what they want out. The gap is somewhere less obvious.

options.t: The inputs.
options.why: Usually named, or at least gestured at. Think about what only you know.

checks.q: You wrote one line, and what came back was generic. What does that mean?

options.t: You need a skill file before it can do this properly.
options.why: A skill helps once you're repeating yourself. Something cheaper fixes this first attempt.

options.t: It's the teachable moment. Add what you left out and go again.
The task is a poor fit for Cowork.
options.why: You haven't tested the task yet. You've tested a one-line brief.

steps.title: Four ways Cowork gets better at your work
steps.cap: You won't start with all four on day one. Set global instructions first, add a project as recurring work surfaces, build a skill when you're tired of re-explaining a process, and bundle a plugin once you have something worth sharing.
steps.teach:
Right now you re-explain yourself every time. These four stop that. Global instructions: who you are and how you work, set once.

Projects: one stream of work, so Claude acts like it's already on the team. Skills: how a specific process should be done, your way. Plugins: your whole role's expertise, bundled.

The more it knows, the more it takes off your plate, and the context you supply once keeps paying off.

checks.q: Someone is a week into Cowork and asks what to set up first.

options.t: A plugin, so everything is in place from the start.
options.why: That's the last of the four, and it bundles things they haven't built yet.

options.t: Global instructions: who you are, carried into every session.
All four, so nothing is missing.
options.why: Each earns its place at a different moment. Setting up all four on day one means guessing at three of them.

checks.q: When is a skill the right thing to reach for?

options.t: When a project has grown too large.
options.why: Size isn't the trigger. Think about repetition rather than volume.

options.t: When you want a teammate to have it too.
options.why: That comes after. Something has to be worth sharing before sharing is the question.

options.t: When you're tired of explaining the same process.

steps.title: Standing context: about you, and about the work
steps.cap: That last one is the difference projects make. Outside a project each session starts fresh; inside one, every conversation adds to what Claude knows, so the next task opens with the client's situation and last week's decisions already in hand.
steps.teach:
Two kinds of standing context. Global instructions are a brief about you, set once in Settings: who you are, your shorthand, how you like output. They apply to every session.

A project is scoped to one stream of work, a client, a recurring report, a launch, and it holds instructions, the folders it works from, and scheduled runs. The difference projects make is the last part: memory. Inside a project, every conversation adds to what Claude knows. Outside one, each session starts fresh.

checks.q: You worked in a project last week and made several decisions. New task, same project. What does it start with?

options.t: The files and instructions you put in, but not the decisions.
options.why: Close, and it undersells it. A project doesn't only hold what you filed.

options.t: The files, the instructions, and the memory it built from those conversations.
Nothing. Memory is a per-conversation thing.
options.why: True of a bare chat. A project does something a chat cannot.

checks.q: Global instructions and a project both carry standing context. What separates them?

options.t: Global instructions are permanent; a project's context expires.
options.why: Neither expires. The difference is about scope rather than lifespan.

options.t: Global instructions are for preferences; a project is for files.
options.why: A project holds far more than files, and instructions do more than set preferences.

options.t: Global instructions cover you everywhere; a project covers one stream of work.

steps.title: A skill is a playbook Claude loads when the task matches
steps.cap: Instructions tell Claude what to do; assets give it the raw materials; references show it what "good" looks like; scripts run the repeatable parts the same way every time. Include what the work needs, nothing more.
steps.teach:
A skill is a playbook. A folder where you write down how one kind of work should be done, once, so Claude does it your way every time. The brief, SKILL.md, is the only required part: what it does, when, and how, written like a runbook for a new colleague.

Add templates as assets, your best past work as references, and a script for the part that must come out identical every time. Claude loads it on its own when the task matches. And you build it by talking: 'I want a skill for the thing I keep re-explaining, walk me through what you need.'

checks.q: A skill folder can hold four things. How many are required?

options.t: One: SKILL.md.
Two: SKILL.md and at least one example of good output.
options.why: Examples help a great deal and are still optional.

options.t: All four, or it won't load.
options.why: Only one is load-bearing. The other three earn their place when the work needs them.

checks.q: There's a script in the skill folder and you can't read code. What do you do?

options.t: Have a developer check it before you use the skill.
options.why: Sensible for anything that touches production, and it dodges the question of where the skill's intelligence actually lives.

options.t: Read the SKILL.md. That's where the thinking is, in plain English.
Delete the script and keep the instructions.
options.why: The script is doing the repeatable part the same way every time. You'd be throwing away the reliable half.

steps.title: A plugin bundles skills around a job
steps.cap: Anthropic publishes plugins for common roles, finance, legal, sales, support. Install one off the shelf, customise it to your templates, or build your own. The expertise travels with the install, not the person. Start with /setup-cowork to find the right one.
steps.teach:
A plugin is a package built around a job. Two kinds. A pipeline: several skills that run in sequence, like pull the actuals, build the variance, draft the board memo.

Or a toolkit: the skills a function reaches for most, bundled so a new teammate installs one thing and has the whole set. The point is the expertise travels with the install, not the person. Anthropic publishes them for finance, legal, sales, support; start with /setup-cowork and it finds the one that fits your work.

videos.label: Cowork and Plugins: Helping enterprises move faster

checks.q: What is a plugin?

options.t: Several skills, plus the connectors and subagents they need, bundled round a job.
A marketplace listing for a skill.
options.why: The marketplace is how it travels, not what it is.

options.t: A skill with the connectors it needs attached.
options.why: Nearly. A plugin is bigger than one playbook.

checks.q: Someone has just built their first skill and asks whether to make it a plugin.

options.t: Yes. A plugin is the proper way to package a skill.
options.why: There's nothing to bundle yet. A plugin gathers several things that already work.

options.t: Not yet. Plugins bundle several skills, so there's nothing to gather.
Yes, because only plugins can be shared with a team.
options.why: A single skill can be handed over on its own.

steps.title: Claude in Chrome, the bridge for tools with no connector
steps.cap: You stay signed in, Claude works in the session you've already authenticated, it can't log in for you. One conversation, both surfaces. (Claude in Chrome may not be available on some enterprise plans.)
steps.teach:
"Some of your tools have no connector: the BI dashboard, the procurement portal, the CRM behind single sign-on. Claude in Chrome is the bridge. It reads and clicks the page in the session you're already signed into, pulls what you need, and hands it back to Cowork to build the deliverable.

One conversation across both. The line that matters: it can't log in for you, you stay signed in, and it asks before sensitive actions." (The deck's caption: you stay signed in; Claude in Chrome may not be available on some enterprise plans.)

videos.label: Claude for Chrome brings AI where you’re already working

checks.q: What is Claude in Chrome for?

options.t: Reading public web pages when Cowork can't reach the internet.
options.why: Cowork isn't cut off from the web. The gap this fills is behind something.

options.t: Vendor portals and dashboards that have no connector.
Anything faster to do in a browser than in Cowork.
options.why: Speed isn't the reason it exists. Think about the systems that offer no other way in.

checks.q: The portal needs a login. What does Claude in Chrome do about that?

options.t: It asks you for the password when it reaches the page.
options.why: It never needs to hold the password at all.

options.t: It signs in with credentials you store in settings.
options.why: It doesn't take your credentials. There's a simpler arrangement that avoids the question.

options.t: It works inside the session you're already signed in to.

steps.title: Claude for Microsoft 365, inside the document
steps.cap: Reach for Cowork when work pulls from many sources and ends in a deliverable; reach for Claude in M365 when you're editing the Office file in place. The two hand off cleanly, and the file is the file in both.
steps.teach:
"The same Claude turns up inside the Office apps as an add-in. In Excel it writes formulas and variance commentary and debugs your #REF errors. In PowerPoint it reads your slide master and builds native, editable charts.

In Word it drafts and reformats in place with tracked changes. In Outlook it triages and drafts replies with the context of the thread. And one conversation carries the context across, the Excel model becomes the deck becomes the email.

Reach for Cowork to build from many sources; reach for M365 when you're editing the file itself." (The deck's caption: the two hand off cleanly, and the file is the file in both.)

videos.label: Collaborate with Claude across Microsoft365 apps

checks.q: You need a first draft that pulls from six different sources, then a careful polish of the Word file. Which tools?

options.t: The Microsoft 365 add-in throughout, since the deliverable is a Word file.
options.why: The add-in works on the file you have open. Pulling six sources together is the other tool's job.

options.t: Cowork throughout. The add-in is for people who won't leave Office.
options.why: That undersells the add-in. Refining a document in place is genuinely better where the document already exists.

options.t: Cowork for the draft, then the Microsoft 365 add-in for the polish.

checks.q: Do Cowork and the Microsoft 365 add-in compete?

options.t: No. One builds the draft from many sources, the other refines the file in place.
Yes. Pick whichever suits how you like to work.
options.why: That frames them as a preference, and most real work runs through both in sequence.

options.t: Yes, and the add-in wins for anything that ends up in Office.
options.why: Where it ends up doesn't decide where it should be built.

steps.title: The folder sets the boundary; the prompt sets the bounds
steps.cap: Most mistakes don't happen because a safeguard failed, they happen because someone clicked through a confirmation that wasn't quite the action they intended. The dialog exists because the action matters; treat it that way.
steps.teach:
"An autonomous tool with file and app access needs guardrails, and most of them are yours to bring. Three layers. Set up: a dedicated folder, not a catch-all; back up anything irreplaceable; test new tasks on copies.

Write the prompt: name destructive verbs precisely, name the bounds, 'only Q3 files', keep it draft-only until you trust it. And in the moment: read the plan before it runs, watch for scope creep, and when a confirmation appears, read it. Most mistakes aren't a safeguard failing, they're someone clicking through a dialog that wasn't quite the action they meant." (The deck's caption: the dialog exists because the action matters, treat it that way.)

checks.q: "What if it does something I didn't want?" What's the floor, before any setup you do yourself?

options.t: It runs everything past you before acting.
options.why: That's the default setting, which you can change. The floor is the thing you can't turn off.

options.t: It always asks before deleting.
It can't touch anything outside the folder.
options.why: True and it's the boundary rather than the floor. Within the folder, one action still always stops to ask.

checks.q: You're setting someone up for their first real run. What's the sensible arrangement?

options.t: Their live working folder, so the result is immediately useful.
options.why: It's also where a mistake costs the most, on the run where they understand it least.

options.t: An empty folder, so nothing can go wrong.
options.why: Nothing can go wrong and nothing can happen either. They learn nothing about their own work.

options.t: A dedicated folder, the irreplaceable backed up, and a copy to test on.

steps.title: An eval is a try-out: with the skill, and without
steps.cap: Built into skill-creator . The bar for shipping isn't perfect evals, it's that the cases you care about pass meaningfully better than the baseline, and you've named the ones you don't yet handle. Change one thing at a time.
steps.teach:
"An eval is just a try-out. Don't let the word scare you. skill-creator runs the same realistic request two ways, once with your skill, once without, and shows you the pair. You read both and answer two questions: would I send the skill version, and if not, what's off?

You say it in plain English, 'too formal', 'skipped the summary', and Claude revises. It's a loop, not a one-time gate. You ship when the cases you care about beat the baseline and you've named the edge cases you don't handle yet." (The deck's caption: change one thing at a time; the bar is meaningfully better than baseline, not perfect.)

checks.q: You've built a skill. How do you find out whether it's any good?

options.t: Run the same prompt with the skill and without it, and compare.
Use it for a fortnight and see whether it feels better.
options.why: You'll have adjusted to it by then, and you'll have nothing to compare against.

options.t: Read it through and check the instructions are complete.
options.why: Worth doing, and it tells you what you intended rather than what comes out.

checks.q: What's the bar an eval has to clear here?

options.t: A test script that runs automatically on each change.
options.why: This one is your judgement, not code. No scripts involved.

options.t: The cases you care about come out meaningfully better than the baseline.
Every case passes.
options.why: That's a higher bar than the work needs and you'd never ship anything.

steps.title: From one laptop to the whole team
steps.cap: Teammates see it in their Directory, labeled as coming from your company; your updates flow to them automatically. Keep it healthy: one named owner, evals before every publish, name skills specifically, review quarterly.
steps.teach:
The payoff: what started on your laptop becomes something the whole team installs. Inside a company, that runs through a private marketplace an admin manages. You hand your plugin to whoever owns it, and they publish it at a level, available to opt into, installed by default, or required for things everyone must run the same way.

Teammates see it in their Directory, labelled as coming from your company, and your updates flow to them automatically. Keep it alive with four habits: one named owner, evals before every publish, specific names, and a quarterly review to retire what nobody runs.

checks.q: Your firm has no private marketplace. Can you still give a teammate your plugin?

options.t: Only if they have the same plan as you.
options.why: The plan gate is on the marketplace, not on the plugin.

options.t: Yes. Export the plugin folder and hand it over.
No. Distribution only works through a marketplace.
options.why: It's a folder. Anything that moves a folder will move it.

checks.q: Who decides that a plugin is installed by default for everyone?

options.t: The person who wrote it.
options.why: Writing it and publishing it to a whole organisation are different jobs with different permissions.

options.t: Anyone on the team, once it's in the marketplace.
options.why: That would make a default nobody agreed to. Publishing has an owner.

options.t: An owner: a team lead, IT, or enablement.
